newsitem.title: UK: More remedial action expected at Ford Europe.
newsitem.headline: More remedial action expected at Ford Europe.

text.p: Ford of Europe's owners in Detroit are losing patience with the rising tide of losses, and will be looking for more cost cuts after action at the Halewood, England plant, analysts said Thursday.
Earlier today Ford UK said it will shed 1,300 jobs from its Halewood plant, and switch production of the 1999 Escort to Germany and Spain.
It is the failure of the Escort rather than problems at the plant which forced Ford to make this decision, analysts said.
Ford of Europe is suffering mainly because people refuse to fall in love with the Escort-the small family car that competes with the Volkswagen Golf and Opel Astra.

According to Professor Krish Bhaskar of the Motor Industry Research Unit in Nice, France, Ford has spent about $2 billion since 1991 redesigning and improving the Escort. At the same time Ford has been forced to spend heavily on advertising and price concessions to stop Escorts clogging up garage forecourts.
The Escort's failure, and the ridiculed styling of the executive class Scorpio, has hammered Ford Europe's bottom line.

"People just didn't like the Escort. It was not as exciting as the competition, and Ford kept on having to revamp it," said Charles Young, director of Automotive Research at J.D.Power-LMC Automotive Forecasting.
Ford Europe lost $472 million in the third quarter of 1996, up from a loss of $320 million in the same 1995 period.
This despite impressive success with the Ford Mondeo family car and the Galaxy multi-purpose vehicle.
The Economist Intelligence Unit says losses will get worse before recovering later this year.
"Although we have been forecasting a significant full year 1996 loss for Ford of Europe for some time, we have now increased this predicted loss to $300 million from $240 million," the E.I.U. said.
"A return to profitability in 1997 is still expected but we have cut this forecast to $400 million from $560 million," the E.I.U. said.
The E.I.U. said Ford Europe's marketing costs are more than twice those of U.S. Ford, accounting for 16.4 percent of revenue compared with 6.8 percent in the U.S. in 1996's third quarter.
"Not surprisingly this has led to renewed speculation that Ford is about to embark on further radical cost cutting to bring the European operations back into profit," the E.I.U. said.

Late last year Ford Motor Co of the U.S. promoted Jacques Nasser to the post of president, Ford Automotive Operations. Included in his remit was Ford of Europe, which he controlled as chairman until 1994.
"Nasser's been drafted back to take charge of the situation which needs active restructuring," said the E.I.U.'s automotive group director Ian Robertson.

Analysts say the outlook for car companies in western Europe is tough. Although sales rose just over 6-1/2 percent last year to 12.8 million, much of this was induced by heavy discounting, and government incentives to replace clunky old polluters.

The prospect for 1997 is stagnation, and more competition from makers in South Korea, Malaysia and India. This means car makers will see little respite from the treadmill of cutting costs and prices to maintain market share.
In 1996 Ford's sales rose 4.2 percent to 1.48 million, but market share dipped to 11.6 percent from 11.9 percent.
